$comment: THE source of truth for Deck's colour. Nothing else should hold a hex.
Four things consume this file and none of them can read a CSS variable at
the moment they need one: Tailwind's theme, the share card (a <canvas>),
the embeddable badge (an SVG served into somebody else's page), and the
handbook's print stylesheet. Before this file existed each of those held
its own hand-copied copy, which is how a palette revert once restored the
token names but left one file on the old values.
Edit here, run `npm run tokens`, and all four regenerate together.
Tokens are named by ROLE, not by hue. `pop` is the bright block whatever
colour it currently is; `deep` is the dark one. That is what lets the
styleguide swap the whole system without touching a single component.
The contract every palette must satisfy is in design/CONTRACT.md and is

lime-slate.label: Lime / Slate
lime-slate.note: Current. High-chroma chartreuse against a dark teal. The loudest of the four; strongest brand recall, least forgiving next to a warm logo.

amber-ink.label: Amber / Ink
amber-ink.note: Warm orange against true black. The most conventional launch-board reading, and the friendliest backdrop for logos of any hue since black is not a colour anyone's brand competes with.

coral-ink.label: Coral / Ink
coral-ink.note: Hot coral against black. Highest energy, reads editorial rather than corporate. Its mark tone is the darkest of the four, so link text sits quieter on the page.

lavender-midnight.label: Lavender / Midnight
lavender-midnight.note: Pale violet against near-black indigo — both lifted from the palette image you sent earlier. The softest of the five: its bright block is the least saturated, so it competes with a logo less than lime or coral, but it also asserts itself least. Its dark block is nearly black, which means the hover has to go lighter rather than darker to stay visible.

cobalt-navy.label: Cobalt / Navy
cobalt-navy.note: Sky blue against deep navy. The calmest option and the most obviously 'interface' — which cuts both ways: it never fights a logo, and it is the hue most likely to look like somebody else's brand.

mono-ink.label: Mono / Ink
mono-ink.note: No hue at all — black, white and the greys between. The interesting constraint is the bright block: because blocks are fixed across both themes, and monochrome has only value to work with, `pop` has to clear 3:1 on a white canvas AND on a near-black one. That leaves a band roughly #7f7f7f to #909090 and nothing else; anything lighter vanishes on white, anything darker vanishes on the dark canvas. So the loudest thing this palette can say is a mid grey, and every bit of emphasis has to come from the 1px border and the hard shadow instead of from colour. That is either the most honest version of this style or proof it needs a hue — which is the question worth looking at here.
